table.text: The study was conducted according to the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki (last update: Brazil, 2013) and was part of a larger research project approved by a local Ethical Committee (CEIIPsi; project code: PE 41 v.2).

The study at UGR was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Granada (1188/CEIH/2020), whereas at UNC the study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychological Research (CEIIPsi -PE 41 v.2).

Other studies have demonstrated that working memory load negatively affects vigilance (Helton and Rusell, 2011). Smit et al. (2004) found that performance in a vigilance task was worse when participants had to detect two stimuli instead of one.

table.text: However, it has also been found that tasks with more salient targets can generate a greater vigilance decrement. Ralph et al. Participants were instructed via email on how to select the task parameters for each session, being unaware of the specific task load and perceptual salience manipulations that were implemented in each session.

In each experimental session, participants completed one of the nine orthogonal combinations of task load (simple, dual, or triple) and perceptual salience (low, standard, or high), in a randomized order by participant.

Before each session, participants were given specific instructions and practice blocks according to the task type, to complete only the sub-task or sub-tasks of the ANTI-Vea of that session, as in Luna, Barttfeld et al. (2022).

table.text: In addition, before and after the experimental task, participants completed a series of self-report questionnaires, that is, similar to the Study 1, the Dundee Stress State Questionnaire (pre-and post-task versions), SAM, DES, the NASA-TLX (Nygren, 1991), and visual analog scales for intentional and spontaneous mind-wandering at different time points of the task.

table.text: Finally, in the triple task condition, which is the standard ANTI-Vea task (Coll-Martín et al., 2024; Luna et al., 2018; Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2021), participants had to respond to all three types of trials (highlighted in orange in Figure 4): to the direction pointed by the target in ANTI trials, to detect the vertical displacement of the target in EV trials, and to stop the countdown as fast as possible in AV trials.

table.text: Four participants were excluded from this analysis due to technical issues resulting in incomplete data.

Higher perceptual salience was associated with largest sensitivity, indicating that participants were better able to discriminate signal from non-signal trials when the target displacement was more salient.

Data from 25 participants were collected at the University of Granada, Spain, where each participant received €60 for their participation, whereas the remaining 25 participants were from the National University of Córdoba, Argentina, and voluntarily participated in the study without receiving any economic or academic compensation.
Participants completed ten online sessions in total.
During this session, the use of the web platforms was explained and participants completed the standard version of the ANTI-Vea (triple task with standard perceptual salience).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In a previous study conducted with the ANTI-Vea (Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022), a summary analysis between experiments showed a between-within interaction with an effect size of 𝜂 𝑝2 = .06 for the change in hits (dependent variable) between task load (betweenparticipant factor with three levels: single/dual/triple) and block (within-participant factor with six levels). Using G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007), the minimum sample size required to observe a similar effect size to the one reported in Luna et al. (2022) was a-priori estimated for the present study, in which a similar design was used (between-participants factor: perceptual salience with three levels, low/standard/high; within-participant factor: block with six levels). Considering a power of 1-β = .95 and an α error = .05, the minimum sample size required to observe an interaction between perceptual salience and block with an effect size of 𝜂 𝑝2 = .06 was N = 84. Anticipating the potential need to exclude some participants from data analysis (following data filtering for standard analyses conducted with the ANTI-Vea, see Luna et al., 2021), we decided to gather data from 90 participants (n = 30 by group).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold"). ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p's > .110", "ps > .05", "p's > .05" ), Text = c("Pairwise comparisons did not show significant differences in the linear component between tasks (all p's > .110).", "For the sake of clarity, the main effect of sample was not observed as significant for 646 hits, FA, sensitivity, or response bias as dependent variable (all ps > .05).", "In all perceptual salience levels, no significant differences were found between the single and the dual task (all p's > .05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: Other studies have demonstrated that working memory load negatively affects vigilance (Helton and Rusell, 2011). Smit et al. (2004) found that performance in a vigilance task was worse when participants had to detect two stimuli instead of one.

However, it has also been found that tasks with more salient targets can generate a greater vigilance decrement. Ralph et al. (2017) compared two vigilance tasks with different levels of demands: an easy task, the Mackworth Clock Test (MCT, Mackworth, 1948), where participants had to detect repetitive stimuli in a monotonous sequence, and a difficult task (Car Task), which simulated driving a car, requiring participants to stay in lane while avoiding obstacles and compensating for wind gusts.
In Study 2, participants completed nine sessions of the online ANTI-Vea (Luna, Roca et al., 2021) in which task load and target salience were manipulated orthogonally.
Participants were assigned to one of three groups according to the perceptual salience of the target (i.e., low, standard, or high).
Participants completed a written informed consent on the LimeSurvey platform before data collection.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental groups according to perceptual salience (low/standard/high) of the EV sub-task in the ANTI-Vea.
In short, participants are instructed to fix their gaze on the fixation point at all times.
Participants are instructed to detect the infrequent displacement by pressing the space bar, in these cases, ignoring the direction indicated by the target (see Figure 1D).
Participants are instructed to stop the millisecond counter as fast as possible by pressing any key from the keyboard (see Figure 1D).
Before experimental blocks, participants completed several practice blocks with and without visual feedback, as in previous studies with the ANTI-Vea (Luna et al., 2018; Luna, Roca, et al., 2021).
After performing the ANTI-Vea, participants completed the Spanish translation (Arquer & Nogareda, 1999) of the short version of the NASA-TLX scale (Nygren, 1991).

Participants were asked to complete the remaining nine experimental sessions in a controlled environment of their choice (quiet, well-lit, and with a stable internet connection), with the speaker volume set to 75% and trying to complete the task at the same time of the day every session (one session per day).

Participants were instructed via email on how to select the task parameters for each session, being unaware of the specific task load and perceptual salience manipulations that were implemented in each session.

In each experimental session, participants completed one of the nine orthogonal combinations of task load (simple, dual, or triple) and perceptual salience (low, standard, or high), in a randomized order by participant.

Before each session, participants were given specific instructions and practice blocks according to the task type, to complete only the sub-task or sub-tasks of the ANTI-Vea of that session, as in Luna, Barttfeld et al. (2022).

In addition, before and after the experimental task, participants completed a series of self-report questionnaires, that is, similar to the Study 1, the Dundee Stress State Questionnaire (pre-and post-task versions), SAM, DES, the NASA-TLX (Nygren, 1991), and visual analog scales for intentional and spontaneous mind-wandering at different time points of the task.

In the single task condition, participants were required to respond only to EV trials by pressing the space bar when the target was vertically displaced (highlighted in green in Figure 4), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials) or to the countdown (i.e., AV trials).

In the dual task condition, in addition to responding to EV trials, participants had to stop the countdown by pressing any key in AV trials (highlighted in blue in Figure 4), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials).

Finally, in the triple task condition, which is the standard ANTI-Vea task (Coll-Martín et al., 2024; Luna et al., 2018; Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2021), participants had to respond to all three types of trials (highlighted in orange in Figure 4): to the direction pointed by the target in ANTI trials, to detect the vertical displacement of the target in EV trials, and to stop the countdown as fast as possible in AV trials.
Four participants were excluded from this analysis due to technical issues resulting in incomplete data.

Higher perceptual salience was associated with largest sensitivity, indicating that participants were better able to discriminate signal from non-signal trials when the target displacement was more salient.

Data from 25 participants were collected at the University of Granada, Spain, where each participant received €60 for their participation, whereas the remaining 25 participants were from the National University of Córdoba, Argentina, and voluntarily participated in the study without receiving any economic or academic compensation.
Participants completed ten online sessions in total.
During this session, the use of the web platforms was explained and participants completed the standard version of the ANTI-Vea (triple task with standard perceptual salience).

text.text: The paper is part of the doctoral thesis by MJA under the supervision of PB, FGL and JL.
MJA received PhD scholarship support from the Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas (CONICET), Argentina.
Preliminary results of this work were presented at the 23 rd Conference of the European Society for Cognitive Psychology (ESCOP) in Porto, Portugal.
FLG was partially supported via a postdoctoral scholarship granted by the CONICET, Argentina.

The vigilance decrement is defined as a progressive loss in the ability to monitor the environment and detect rare but critical stimuli, as evidenced by an increase in erroneous and slower responses over time (Davies & Parasuraman, 1982).
text.formatted: The vigilance decrement is defined as a progressive loss in the ability to monitor the environment and detect rare but critical stimuli, as evidenced by an increase in erroneous and slower responses over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Davies & Parasuraman, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: The vigilance decrement can lead to mild consequences, such as missing a reading, or severe ones, such as a traffic accident (Baysari et al., 2008; Edkins & Pollock, 1997).
text.formatted: The vigilance decrement can lead to mild consequences, such as missing a reading, or severe ones, such as a traffic accident <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baysari et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Edkins & Pollock, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The study of vigilance has gained considerable interest in understanding the causes and mechanisms associated with the vigilance decrement and to optimize performance in prolonged tasks (Thomson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The study of vigilance has gained considerable interest in understanding the causes and mechanisms associated with the vigilance decrement and to optimize performance in prolonged tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Several theoretical models have been proposed, which currently might be grouped into two relatively opposing frameworks: overload and underload theories (Thomson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Several theoretical models have been proposed, which currently might be grouped into two relatively opposing frameworks: overload and underload theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For decades, the most widely accepted explanation for the vigilance decrement has been the overload theory based on the resource depletion hypothesis (Warm et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For decades, the most widely accepted explanation for the vigilance decrement has been the overload theory based on the resource depletion hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Warm et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: According to this view, attention relies on limited resources that are consumed during sustained activity and are not quickly replenished (Dillard et al., 2019; Grier et al., 2003).
text.formatted: According to this view, attention relies on limited resources that are consumed during sustained activity and are not quickly replenished <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dillard et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Grier et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In general, the resource depletion hypothesis posits that vigilance tasks-because they require substantial mental effort-consume more resources and produce a greater vigilance decrement.
However, recent research has suggested that these resources may be renewable (Helton & Wen, 2023).
text.formatted: However, recent research has suggested that these resources may be renewable <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Helton & Wen, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, underload theories include proposals such as the mindlessness hypothesis (Robertson et al., 1997), the resource control hypothesis (Thomson et al., 2015), and the mind-wandering hypothesis (Smallwood & Schooler, 2006).
text.formatted: In contrast, underload theories include proposals such as the mindlessness hypothesis <ref type="bibr">(Robertson et al., 1997)</ref>, the resource control hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>, and the mind-wandering hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Smallwood & Schooler, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, the mindwandering hypothesis, unlike the resource depletion account, argues that the vigilance decrement does not result from a depletion of resources, but rather from the redistribution of attentional resources toward irrelevant internal thoughts (i.e., mind-wandering).
From mindwandering hypothesis, vigilance tasks are considered undemanding, monotonous, and cognitively unstimulating, which facilitates attentional disengagement (Neigel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: From mindwandering hypothesis, vigilance tasks are considered undemanding, monotonous, and cognitively unstimulating, which facilitates attentional disengagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Neigel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the mind-wandering hypothesis predicts that more demanding or more engaging tasks should reduce the likelihood of mind-wandering and, in turn, mitigate the vigilance decrement (Smallwood, 2010), whereas boring or low-demand tasks should promote a faster withdrawal of attention and a more pronounced decline in performance over time (Thomson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Consequently, the mind-wandering hypothesis predicts that more demanding or more engaging tasks should reduce the likelihood of mind-wandering and, in turn, mitigate the vigilance decrement <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Smallwood, 2010)</ref>, whereas boring or low-demand tasks should promote a faster withdrawal of attention and a more pronounced decline in performance over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Numerous empirical studies have tested the assumptions of the resource depletion and mind-wandering hypotheses by manipulating task characteristics, such as load and/or physical features of stimuli, with the latter often operationalized through perceptual salience (Esterman & Rothlein, 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2017; Helton & Warm, 2008; Seli et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Numerous empirical studies have tested the assumptions of the resource depletion and mind-wandering hypotheses by manipulating task characteristics, such as load and/or physical features of stimuli, with the latter often operationalized through perceptual salience <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Esterman & Rothlein, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Gonçalves et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Helton & Warm, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Seli et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, it appears that both theories are currently unable to explain the reported findings (Esterman & Rothlein, 2019; Neigel et al., 2020; Thomson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: However, it appears that both theories are currently unable to explain the reported findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Esterman & Rothlein, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Neigel et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, task load is manipulated by varying the number of tasks performed simultaneously and the number of instructions that need to be maintained.
Several studies show that performing a dual task affects vigilance more than performing a single task.

For example, Head and Helton (2014) found that hits in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) were worse when combined with a verbal memory task, compared to performing the SART alone. Epling et al. (2016) also observed a greater vigilance decrement when a semantic vigilance task was combined with a word recall task.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Head and Helton (2014)</ref> found that hits in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) were worse when combined with a verbal memory task, compared to performing the SART alone. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Epling et al. (2016)</ref> also observed a greater vigilance decrement when a semantic vigilance task was combined with a word recall task.

text.text: Other studies have demonstrated that working memory load negatively affects vigilance (Helton and Rusell, 2011). Smit et al. (2004) found that performance in a vigilance task was worse when participants had to detect two stimuli instead of one.
text.formatted: Other studies have demonstrated that working memory load negatively affects vigilance <ref type="bibr">(Helton and Rusell, 2011)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Smit et al. (2004)</ref> found that performance in a vigilance task was worse when participants had to detect two stimuli instead of one.

text.text: Overall, these results support the resource depletion theory, which proposes that higher cognitive demands deplete limited resources more quickly.
However, other studies indicate that increasing task load do not necessarily impair target's detection in the vigilance task and, in some cases, may mitigate the vigilance decrement.

In this regard, for example, a correlational pattern was observed by Seli et al. (2016), who found that unintentional mind-wandering was more frequent during more demanding tasks, whereas intentional mind-wandering was more common during easier ones.
text.formatted: In this regard, for example, a correlational pattern was observed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Seli et al. (2016)</ref>, who found that unintentional mind-wandering was more frequent during more demanding tasks, whereas intentional mind-wandering was more common during easier ones.

text.text: Building on this, Seli et al. (2018) tested the mind-wandering hypothesis by experimentally manipulating task difficulty: including a working memory component in the difficult condition and using a simple vigilance task in the easy one.
text.formatted: Building on this, <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Seli et al. (2018)</ref> tested the mind-wandering hypothesis by experimentally manipulating task difficulty: including a working memory component in the difficult condition and using a simple vigilance task in the easy one.

text.text: Participants' responses were more accurate and faster in the easy condition, confirming the effectiveness of the manipulation.
These results suggest that tasks with lower cognitive demands support more stable vigilance performance.
Although the vigilance decrement was not directly measured, the authors examined in intentional and unintentional mind-wandering as a function of task difficulty.
Overall, mind-wandering rates were lower in the easy task, though more often intentional-likely because the task required less cognitive control.
In contrast, unintentional mind-wandering was associated with reduced performance in the difficult task.
Also, Epling et al. (2019) found that vigilance remained stable when a semantic vigilance task was combined with a narrative memory task.
text.formatted: Also, <ref type="bibr">Epling et al. (2019)</ref> found that vigilance remained stable when a semantic vigilance task was combined with a narrative memory task.

text.text: Similarly, in air traffic control tasks, performing two tasks simultaneously did not reduce vigilance compared to performing only one (Pop et al., 2012; Stearman and Durso, 2016; see also Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, in air traffic control tasks, performing two tasks simultaneously did not reduce vigilance compared to performing only one <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Pop et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Stearman and Durso, 2016</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These results seem to contradict the resource depletion hypothesis and could be better explained by the mindwandering hypothesis.
The lack of consensus in the results on the effects of task load on vigilance complicates agreement on theoretical explanations for vigilance decrement.
While some findings align with the resource depletion hypothesis, others are better accounted for by the mind-wandering hypothesis.
Alternatively, task demands may be modulated by perceptual salience of the target stimuli.
Evidence shows that more difficult tasks tend to yield worse overall performance and a greater vigilance decrement.
Gómez Iñiguez et al. (2000) observed that in a difficult task (with more distractors), there were fewer hits and more false alarms.
text.formatted: Gómez <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Iñiguez et al. (2000)</ref> observed that in a difficult task (with more distractors), there were fewer hits and more false alarms.

text.text: Similarly, Helton and Warm (2008) found that tasks with higher perceptual salience, i.e., easier tasks, led to reduced vigilance decrement.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Helton and Warm (2008)</ref> found that tasks with higher perceptual salience, i.e., easier tasks, led to reduced vigilance decrement.

text.text: These findings support the resource depletion theory, which suggests that perceptually more demanding tasks require more resources, depleting them more quickly.
In general, these show that lower perceptual salience increases processing demands and tends to exacerbate the vigilance decrement.

However, it has also been found that tasks with more salient targets can generate a greater vigilance decrement. Ralph et al. (2017) compared two vigilance tasks with different levels of demands: an easy task, the Mackworth Clock Test (MCT, Mackworth, 1948), where participants had to detect repetitive stimuli in a monotonous sequence, and a difficult task (Car Task), which simulated driving a car, requiring participants to stay in lane while avoiding obstacles and compensating for wind gusts.
text.formatted: However, it has also been found that tasks with more salient targets can generate a greater vigilance decrement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Ralph et al. (2017)</ref> compared two vigilance tasks with different levels of demands: an easy task, the Mackworth Clock Test (MCT, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Mackworth, 1948)</ref>, where participants had to detect repetitive stimuli in a monotonous sequence, and a difficult task (Car Task), which simulated driving a car, requiring participants to stay in lane while avoiding obstacles and compensating for wind gusts.

text.text: Although the Car Task was perceived as more demanding, a vigilance decrement only occurred in the easy task.
This supports the mind-wandering theory, as more engaging and demanding tasks seem to reduce taskunrelated thoughts and help maintain performance.
It is also important to note that vigilance theories have been developed using simple experimental tasks, such as the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) or the MCT.

Although these paradigms allow for precise experimental control, their extremely simple and monotonous nature limits their ability to capture how vigilance unfolds in more dynamic or realistic contexts (Thomson et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Although these paradigms allow for precise experimental control, their extremely simple and monotonous nature limits their ability to capture how vigilance unfolds in more dynamic or realistic contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Thomson et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In an attempt to overcome these limitations, Szalma et al. (2014) developed a video game-based vigilance task that incorporated continuous movement through a complex and perceptually rich virtual environment.
text.formatted: In an attempt to overcome these limitations, <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Szalma et al. (2014)</ref> developed a video game-based vigilance task that incorporated continuous movement through a complex and perceptually rich virtual environment.

text.text: This approach represented an improvement over tasks such as the SART and the MCT by offering greater ecological validity and a less artificial context.

However, this same characteristic also introduced an important limitation: although the task reproduced subjective indicators typically associated with vigilance (e.g., increased distress and reduced engagement), the vigilance decrement was not consistently observed, likely because the richer and more engaging environment reduced the monotony that usually triggers such deterioration.
Moreover, simple vigilance tasks do not include additional measures of other attentional or vigilance components at the same time (Tkachenko & Dinges, 2018).
text.formatted: Moreover, simple vigilance tasks do not include additional measures of other attentional or vigilance components at the same time <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Tkachenko & Dinges, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, when task load is manipulated, researchers often rely on different tasks (Epling et al., 2019; Head & Helton, 2014; Ralph et al., 2017) that vary in the variables assessed, the duration of the trials, and the characteristics of the stimuli.
text.formatted: Furthermore, when task load is manipulated, researchers often rely on different tasks <ref type="bibr">(Epling et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Head & Helton, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Ralph et al., 2017)</ref> that vary in the variables assessed, the duration of the trials, and the characteristics of the stimuli.

text.text: Consequently, the observed variations are difficult to compare among them, as task load is manipulated via different task parameters across studies.

A new tool for measuring multiple attentional and vigilance components in a single session has been developed by our lab: the ANTI-Vea task (Attentional Networks Test for Interactions and Vigilance -executive and arousal components; Luna et al., 2018;  https://anti-vea.ugr.es/).
text.formatted: A new tool for measuring multiple attentional and vigilance components in a single session has been developed by our lab: the ANTI-Vea task (Attentional Networks Test for Interactions and Vigilance -executive and arousal components; <ref type="bibr">Luna et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> <ref type="url" target="https://anti-vea.ugr.es/">https://anti-vea.ugr.es/</ref>).

text.text: The task captures the decrement on two vigilance components: (a) executive vigilance (EV), as the ability to monitor the environment to detect infrequent but critical signals, requiring higher-order cognitive processing such as updating working memory, making decisions, executing accurate responses to targets, and inhibiting responses to non-targets according to task goals (Hemmerich et al., 2025); and (b) arousal vigilance (AV), as the ability to maintain a fast response to an intermittent stimulus that always requires a response, which requires less cognitive control and facilitates a more automatic performance.
text.formatted: The task captures the decrement on two vigilance components: (a) executive vigilance (EV), as the ability to monitor the environment to detect infrequent but critical signals, requiring higher-order cognitive processing such as updating working memory, making decisions, executing accurate responses to targets, and inhibiting responses to non-targets according to task goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hemmerich et al., 2025)</ref>; and (b) arousal vigilance (AV), as the ability to maintain a fast response to an intermittent stimulus that always requires a response, which requires less cognitive control and facilitates a more automatic performance.

text.text: Importantly for our goals in the current study, the ANTI-Vea can be understood as a triple task that evaluates vigilance decrement under certain task load.

In particular, this task integrates three type of trials, requiring different response sets: (a) the ANTI task, in which participants need to respond to the direction of a central arrow, surrounded by two more arrows on each side, and allows measuring the main effects and interactions between phasic alertness, orienting, and cognitive control (Petersen & Posner, 2012); (b) a signal detection task, similar to the SART, to assess the EV -by detecting an infrequent vertical shift of the central target arrow (present in 20% of the trials); and (c) a simple reaction time task, similar to the PVT, to measure AV in which a millisecond counter appears on the screen and participants must stop it as quickly as possible by pressing any key.
text.formatted: In particular, this task integrates three type of trials, requiring different response sets: (a) the ANTI task, in which participants need to respond to the direction of a central arrow, surrounded by two more arrows on each side, and allows measuring the main effects and interactions between phasic alertness, orienting, and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Petersen & Posner, 2012)</ref>; (b) a signal detection task, similar to the SART, to assess the EV -by detecting an infrequent vertical shift of the central target arrow (present in 20% of the trials); and (c) a simple reaction time task, similar to the PVT, to measure AV in which a millisecond counter appears on the screen and participants must stop it as quickly as possible by pressing any key.

text.text: Several studies have replicated the validity and reliability of the ANTI-Vea across different experimental contexts (e.g., Coll-Martín et al., 2021; Luna, Roca et al., 2021), including online versions of the task (https://anti-vea.ugr.es/).
text.formatted: Several studies have replicated the validity and reliability of the ANTI-Vea across different experimental contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Coll-Martín et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Luna, Roca et al., 2021)</ref>, including online versions of the task (<ref type="url" target="https://anti-vea.ugr.es/">https://anti-vea.ugr.es/</ref>).

text.text: Critically, these investigations have shown that measures obtained in online sessions outside the laboratory are comparable to those obtained under standard laboratory conditions.
In both formats, the EV decrement is reflected by a reduction in hits over time.
Considering the advantages of the ANTI-Vea task, Luna, Barttfeld et al. (2022) manipulated task load in the ANTI-Vea task by varying the number of tasks to be performed simultaneously.
text.formatted: Considering the advantages of the ANTI-Vea task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Luna, Barttfeld et al. (2022)</ref> manipulated task load in the ANTI-Vea task by varying the number of tasks to be performed simultaneously.

text.text: They found that the dual-task condition, in which participants only had to respond to the EV and AV trials, mitigated the EV decrement, maintaining hit rates stable over time, compared to the single-task (i.e., when they only had to respond to EV trials) and triple-task conditions, where the typical EV decrement was observed.
However, task load did not affect AV.

The present study aimed to examine the effects of perceptual salience and task load on the vigilance decrement by using a task paradigm that enables both factors to be manipulated within a single, integrated task.

By employing the ANTI-Vea, which comprises several subtasks performed under identical task parameters, perceptual salience and task load were varied by manipulating only a single task parameter for each factor.
To this end, we conducted two studies and a reanalysis of a pooled dataset.
Studies 1 and 2 were pre-registered on OSF, including objectives, hypotheses, procedure and design, sample size estimation, and data analysis plan.

Note that, however, these pre-registrations included hypotheses and analyses regarding additional dependent variables collected through the ANTI-Vea task that are not part of the main goal of the present study.
Here, we will only report measures collected through the EV sub-task of the ANTI-Vea, as it is the only sub-task in which perceptual salience and task load were manipulated across studies.

In Study 1, the perceptual salience of the target (i.e., magnitude of the vertical displacement to be detected) was manipulated between participants at three levels, to examine whether performance (hits, FA, sensitivity and response bias) over time benefits or rather is hindered by different levels of target salience (Gómez Iñiguez et al., 2000; Helton & Warm, 2008; Seli et al., 2018).

text.text: This re-analysis will enable us to further examine the effects of perceptual salience and task load on vigilance through data from a large sample size (N = 238).

The present study aimed to examine the EV decrement via the online ANTI-Vea task as a function of different levels of perceptual salience of the target, to test some of the predictions of vigilance decrement models.
Participants were assigned to one of three groups according to the perceptual salience of the target (i.e., low, standard, or high).
Predictions were opposite for each theoretical account.

According to the resource depletion hypothesis, it was expected that the lowest level of perceptual salience (i.e., highest difficulty to detect the target) would increase task demands and therefore hinder overall and time-on-task EV performance (hits, FA, sensitivity and response bias).
In contrast, following mind-wandering hypothesis it might be expected that a high level of perceptual salience would reduce task demands, therefore facilitating task disengagement.
Consequently, a perceptually less demanding task would lead to a larger EV decrement over time.
This study was pre-registered on OSF (https://osf.io/v3j5s/wiki/home/).

text.text: Ninety healthy young adults (61 women; age: M = 27.74, SD = 5.16), who were undergraduate students from the City of Córdoba, Argentina, volunteered to participate in the present study.
All of them had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Participants completed a written informed consent on the LimeSurvey platform before data collection.

The study was conducted according to the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki (last update: Brazil, 2013) and was part of a larger research project approved by a local Ethical Committee (CEIIPsi; project code: PE 41 v.2).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental groups according to perceptual salience (low/standard/high) of the EV sub-task in the ANTI-Vea.
Due to technical issues, data from 6 participants could not be included in the data analysis.

Thus, the final sample was of 84 participants (i.e., as a-priori estimated), who were part of the experimental groups as follows: n = 28 in the low, n = 30 in the standard, and n = 26 in the high perceptual salience task group.

Procedure and Design Participants received three web links via email to complete the procedure of the study in the following order: (a) the informed consent and a series of self-reported questionnaires in LimeSurvey (i.e., the Spanish version of the Mind Wandering-Deliberated/Mind Wandering-Spontaneous scales, the Discrete Emotional Scale [DES], and the Self-Assessment Manikin (c) another series of self-reported questionnaires on LimeSurvey to be completed post-task (i.e., NASA-TLX, thought identification question, DES, and SAM).
With exception of the NASA-TLX, the inclusion of the remaining aforementioned self-reported questionnaires is, however, part of larger research project, and will be reported elsewhere.

The ANTI-Vea comprises three embedded sub-tasks, which are randomly completed across three type of trials: (a) ANTI, a flanker task with an auditory warning signal and an exogenous visual cue, suitable to assess phasic alertness, orienting, and executive control as in the ANTI task of Callejas et al. (2004); (b) EV, a signal-detection task like the Mackworth Clock Test (Mackworth, 1948) suitable to assess the EV decrement; and (c) AV, a RT task that mimics the PVT (Lim & Dinges, 2008), suitable to measure the AV decrement.

text.text: Instead, in the low salience task, the vertical displacement was fixed at 5 px, while in the high salience task was fixed at 14 px.

Importantly, to increase the difficulty of detecting the target displacement in EV trials, small random displacements (±2 px, applied to both the horizontal and vertical axes) were added to the position of stimuli.
These displacements affected both the target and distractors in ANTI trials, but only the distractors in EV trials, wherein the target was always vertically displaced at its predefined level.
The experimental procedure comprised six consecutive blocks without breaks of 80 randomly presented trials (48 ANTI, 16 EV, and 16 AV), thus measuring vigilance in a period of 32 min 48 sec.
Before experimental blocks, participants completed several practice blocks with and without visual feedback, as in previous studies with the ANTI-Vea (Luna et al., 2018; Luna, Roca, et al., 2021).

text.formatted: After performing the ANTI-Vea, participants completed the Spanish translation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arquer & Nogareda, 1999)</ref> of the short version of the NASA-TLX scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Nygren, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The short NASA-TLX assesses the mental workload perceived about the task performed across six items (i.e., mental, physical, and temporal demands, effort required, perceived performance, and level of frustration) that are rated on a scale between 0 and 20.
A summary score of mental workload is obtained by summing the ratings of the six items.

The NASA-TLX has shown acceptable reliability scores (split-half and Cronbach's α coefficients > .80; et al., 2005), and has been extensively used to assess mental workload (Grier, 2015; Hart, 2006), and specifically also widely used to assess the perceived mental workload associated with the vigilance decrement (Grier et al., 2003; Helton & Warm, 2008; Warm et al., 2008).

The results from Study 1 showed that increasing the salience of the signal was associated with a significant improvement in Ev.
Specifically, the high-salience condition showed a higher proportion of hits and a lower FA rate compared to the low-and standard-salience conditions.

These findings support the idea that greater perceptual salience of relevant stimuli, achieved by reducing perceptual task demands, helps maintain a more stable level of vigilance (Helton & Warm, 2008).
text.formatted: These findings support the idea that greater perceptual salience of relevant stimuli, achieved by reducing perceptual task demands, helps maintain a more stable level of vigilance <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Helton & Warm, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the low-and standard salience conditions replicated the classic deterioration pattern observed in the ANTI-Vea task, characterized by a progressive decline in hit rates.
Note, however, that a similar effect over time was observed for the three levels of perceptual salience with sensitivity (A′) or response bias (B″) measures.
As expected, perceptual salience manipulations did not significantly affect AV measures, as shown in the supplementary material, replicating prior findings (Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As expected, perceptual salience manipulations did not significantly affect AV measures, as shown in the supplementary material, replicating prior findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that, although increased salience of relevant stimuli is effective in supporting goal-directed attention, it does not influence the ability to maintain a general state of alertness to unpredictable temporal signals.
Despite the above-mentioned differences in EV indices, perceived mental workload, as indexed by the global NASA-TLX score, did not vary as a function of perceptual salience.

Participants reported comparable workload after completing the vigilance task across all salience conditions, indicating that the benefits of increased perceptual salience were not accompanied by subjective reductions in workload.

This dissociation between objective performance and subjective workload runs counter to predictions derived from the resource depletion hypothesis and suggests that perceptual facilitation may improve vigilance efficiency without substantially altering perceived task demands.

Building on the results obtained in Study 1 on signal salience, as well as on evidence from a different study showing effects of task load on EV performance (Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022), Study 2 aims to replicate and extend these findings by combining the two dimensions orthogonally in a full within-participant design.
text.formatted: Building on the results obtained in Study 1 on signal salience, as well as on evidence from a different study showing effects of task load on EV performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022)</ref>, Study 2 aims to replicate and extend these findings by combining the two dimensions orthogonally in a full within-participant design.

text.text: Specifically, we examined how different levels of task load (elicited by a single, dual, or triple task, as in Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022) and the target's perceptual salience (low, standard, or high, as in Study 1) would modulate the EV decrement over time, as measured via adapted versions of the online ANTI-Vea task.
text.formatted: Specifically, we examined how different levels of task load (elicited by a single, dual, or triple task, as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022)</ref> and the target's perceptual salience (low, standard, or high, as in Study 1) would modulate the EV decrement over time, as measured via adapted versions of the online ANTI-Vea task.

text.text: This approach allows for the examination of not only the main effects of task load and the target's salience but also their potential interactions.
We anticipated different predictions according to the resource depletion hypothesis and mind-wandering hypothesis regarding the effects of task load and perceptual salience on the EV decrement.

Following the resource depletion hypothesis, the highest overall hit rate and no decrease over time of hits in low demand task conditions was predicted-namely, the single task and high perceptual salience condition-compared to the high demand task conditions-that is, the triple task and the low perceptual salience condition.
In contrast, according to the mind-wandering theory, it is expected that a less demanding task could increase task monotony and therefore exacerbate the vigilance decrement.

Thus, probably a larger decrement would be observed in the single task load condition and in the high perceptual salience condition, than in more demanding conditions, such as the triple task and the low perceptual salience.
We also expected to replicate outcomes observed in previous studies conducted in our lab.
Following Luna, Barttfeld, et al. (2022), we expected that task load would modulate the EV decrement, at least in the standard salience condition.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Luna, Barttfeld, et al. (2022)</ref>, we expected that task load would modulate the EV decrement, at least in the standard salience condition.

text.text: In particular, we expected to observe a similar decrement in the single-and triple-task conditions, but no significant change across time-on-task in hit rate in the dual-task condition, replicating the pattern reported by Luna, Barttfeld, et al. (2022).
text.formatted: In particular, we expected to observe a similar decrement in the single-and triple-task conditions, but no significant change across time-on-task in hit rate in the dual-task condition, replicating the pattern reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Luna, Barttfeld, et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, following the outcomes observed in Study 1, we hypothesized that perceptual salience would modulate the vigilance decrement specifically in the triple task condition, showing no significant change in hit rate in the high salience condition but pronounced decrements in the standard and low salience conditions.
We also expected a higher FA rate in the low compared to the standard and high perceptual salience conditions in the triple task load condition, as reported in Study 1.

text.text: Importantly, data from this session were not included in the analyses.

Participants were asked to complete the remaining nine experimental sessions in a controlled environment of their choice (quiet, well-lit, and with a stable internet connection), with the speaker volume set to 75% and trying to complete the task at the same time of the day every session (one session per day).

Participants were instructed via email on how to select the task parameters for each session, being unaware of the specific task load and perceptual salience manipulations that were implemented in each session.
The following sessions were conducted on different days, encouraging participants to complete the next session in an interval between 24 to 72 hours from the last session, if possible.

In each experimental session, participants completed one of the nine orthogonal combinations of task load (simple, dual, or triple) and perceptual salience (low, standard, or high), in a randomized order by participant.
The experimental blocks lasted 32 minutes and 48 seconds, consisting of six consecutive blocks of 80 trials (48 ANTI, 16 EV, and 16 AV), presented randomly and without breaks.

Before each session, participants were given specific instructions and practice blocks according to the task type, to complete only the sub-task or sub-tasks of the ANTI-Vea of that session, as in Luna, Barttfeld et al. (2022).

text.text: In addition, before and after the experimental task, participants completed a series of self-report questionnaires, that is, similar to the Study 1, the Dundee Stress State Questionnaire (pre-and post-task versions), SAM, DES, the NASA-TLX (Nygren, 1991), and visual analog scales for intentional and spontaneous mind-wandering at different time points of the task.

text.text: Full details of these measures and their use are reported elsewhere in relation to the objectives of a larger research project.
Due to unknown reasons, 16 participants involuntarily repeated at least one of the nine sessions.
To complete the nine sessions of the experimental design, 9 participants from UGR and 7 from UNC completed an additional session and one from UGR completed four additional sessions.
Only the data from the second session were retained for analyses.
The design of the ANTI-Vea task was the same as in Study 1.

However, here, an additional manipulation of task load was introduced through task instructions, while keeping the stimuli and their duration constant across all conditions (as depicted in Figure 1A and 1B).
text.formatted: However, here, an additional manipulation of task load was introduced through task instructions, while keeping the stimuli and their duration constant across all conditions (as depicted in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref> and 1B).

text.text: Task load was varied at three levels, replicating the manipulation in Luna, Barttfeld et al.

In the single task condition, participants were required to respond only to EV trials by pressing the space bar when the target was vertically displaced (highlighted in green in Figure 4), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials) or to the countdown (i.e., AV trials).
text.formatted: In the single task condition, participants were required to respond only to EV trials by pressing the space bar when the target was vertically displaced (highlighted in green in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials) or to the countdown (i.e., AV trials).

text.text: In the dual task condition, in addition to responding to EV trials, participants had to stop the countdown by pressing any key in AV trials (highlighted in blue in Figure 4), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials).
text.formatted: In the dual task condition, in addition to responding to EV trials, participants had to stop the countdown by pressing any key in AV trials (highlighted in blue in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>), while not responding when the target was not displaced (i.e., ANTI trials).

text.text: Finally, in the triple task condition, which is the standard ANTI-Vea task (Coll-Martín et al., 2024; Luna et al., 2018; Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2021), participants had to respond to all three types of trials (highlighted in orange in Figure 4): to the direction pointed by the target in ANTI trials, to detect the vertical displacement of the target in EV trials, and to stop the countdown as fast as possible in AV trials.
text.formatted: Finally, in the triple task condition, which is the standard ANTI-Vea task <ref type="bibr">(Coll-Martín et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Luna et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2021)</ref>, participants had to respond to all three types of trials (highlighted in orange in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>): to the direction pointed by the target in ANTI trials, to detect the vertical displacement of the target in EV trials, and to stop the countdown as fast as possible in AV trials.

To analyze the effects of perceptual salience and task load on the EV decrement, linear mixed-effects models (LME) were used.
Analyses were conducted in R 4.2.0 (R Core Team, 2024) with RStudio 2022.02.3 (Posit, 2024), employing the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

text.text: The models included block (6 levels), perceptual salience (low, standard, high), task load (single, dual, triple), and sample (UGR or UNC) as fixed effects.
Random effects for participants and number of sessions were included to account for their variability.
Although LME models were not specifically anticipated in our pre-registered protocol, we decided to add random effects given the different number of sessions completed by participants.
Note that dependent and independent variables (i.e., fixed effects) were included as anticipated in our pre-registered protocol.
LME models were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood and degrees of freedom were estimated using the Satterthwaite method.
Effect sizes for post hoc comparisons were calculated using the effectsize package (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Effect sizes for post hoc comparisons were calculated using the effectsize package <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ben-Shachar et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To assess performance decline over time, hits, FA, sensitivity, and response bias were calculated as in Study 1 and included as dependent variable in separated LME models.
Main effects and interactions were examined using ANOVAs on each fitted model.
Mental workload, indexed by the NASA -TLX score, was analyzed using a repeatedmeasures ANOVA, with perceptual salience and task load as within-participant factors.
Four participants were excluded from this analysis due to technical issues resulting in incomplete data.

text.text: The results of Study 2 revealed clear main effects of both experimental manipulations, perceptual salience and task load.

Consistent with the findings from Study 1, perceptual salience modulated overall hits and false alarms: participants detected more targets and made fewer false alarms when the target stimuli in the high salience condition.
Regarding the preregistered hypothesis that FA rates would be higher in the low salience condition than in standard and high salience ones, the current outcomes replicated those of Study 1.
These results could support the predictions of the resource depletion hypothesis, which posits that less salient stimuli increase task demands.
This, in turn, leads to greater consumption of attentional resources and consequently poorer performance (Warm et al., 2008; Helton & Warm, 2008).
text.formatted: This, in turn, leads to greater consumption of attentional resources and consequently poorer performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Warm et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Helton & Warm, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation, however, is not supported by the results observed for sensitivity (A′), as no corresponding effect was observed.
Importantly, no modulation of perceptual salience over the EV decrement was observed with any dependent variable.
Subjective workload measures converged with these performance effects.

Specifically, NASA-TLX scores were higher in the low salience condition compared to the high salience condition, indicating that reduced perceptual salience was experienced as more mentally demanding.
This pattern supports the interpretation that low salience increases perceived effort, even in the absence of changes in sensitivity.

On the other hand, the manipulation of task load showed a non-linear pattern on hits: the dual-task condition led to better hit rates than both the single and triple-task conditions, suggesting a benefit of maintaining a moderate level of mental workload.

This interpretation is strongly supported by the NASA-TLX results, which showed substantially higher workload in the triple-task condition compared to the single-task condition, indicating that the task load manipulation effectively altered perceived mental demand.

The lower hit rates observed in the single-task condition are consistent with the mind-wandering hypothesis, which proposes that low task demands facilitate attentional disengagement and mind-wandering (Seli et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The lower hit rates observed in the single-task condition are consistent with the mind-wandering hypothesis, which proposes that low task demands facilitate attentional disengagement and mind-wandering <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Seli et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the decline in hit rates in the triple-task condition is more consistent with the resources depletion account, according to which excessive task demands may exceed available cognitive resources.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the relationship between task load and vigilance decrement is better characterized by an inverted-U-shape pattern, whereby both insufficient and excessive workload impair hit rates, rather than by a single underload-based explanation (Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Taken together, these findings suggest that the relationship between task load and vigilance decrement is better characterized by an inverted-U-shape pattern, whereby both insufficient and excessive workload impair hit rates, rather than by a single underload-based explanation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this inverted-U-shape pattern was observed at the level of hits, while no corresponding differences were found in A′.
This suggests that the task load manipulation could influence response bias rather than sensitivity.

Recent work on vigilance tasks has highlighted that, particularly in modern paradigms characterized by very low FA, performance decrements may predominantly reflect shifts in response bias rather than changes in sensitivity (Thomson et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Recent work on vigilance tasks has highlighted that, particularly in modern paradigms characterized by very low FA, performance decrements may predominantly reflect shifts in response bias rather than changes in sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Thomson et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, moderate levels of task demand may promote a more optimal response criterion-supporting sustained engagement-whereas both low and high workload may bias participants toward a more conservative response criterion, leading to reduced hit rates.

This view is supported by previous research indicating that both active fatigue (associated with high load) and passive fatigue (associated with low stimulation) can impair performance in different ways, depending on how individuals regulate mental effort (Saxby et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This view is supported by previous research indicating that both active fatigue (associated with high load) and passive fatigue (associated with low stimulation) can impair performance in different ways, depending on how individuals regulate mental effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Saxby et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a study in semi-automated driving contexts has shown that vigilance decrements emerge when mental workload is too low, highlighting the risks of sustained attention failures under underload conditions (McWilliams & Ward, 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, a study in semi-automated driving contexts has shown that vigilance decrements emerge when mental workload is too low, highlighting the risks of sustained attention failures under underload conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(McWilliams & Ward, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, maintaining an optimal level of cognitive demand may be critical for sustaining attention, as suggested by both theoretical models and empirical findings.
Nevertheless, and critically, despite these main effects of task load, no modulation over the EV decrement was observed.

Additionally, a significant interaction between perceptual salience and task load was observed: under low-salience conditions, lower-load tasks (single and dual) supported better performance in hits and FA compared to the triple-task condition.
However, this effect diminished as salience increased, suggesting that more efficient perceptual processing may partially compensate for the detrimental effects of high task load.
This interaction highlights the importance of considering multiple sources of task demands when studying vigilance decrement.
Importantly, despite these effects on overall performance, no significant interactions were found between time-on-task and the task load and perceptual salience manipulations.
This suggests that while these variables affect the overall level of performance, they do not substantially change the temporal trajectory of vigilance decrement.

Taken together, these findings underscore the need for more integrative models capable of explaining how task load and perceptual salience interact to influence both performance levels and attentional stability during prolonged tasks.
They also highlight the utility of the ANTI-Vea paradigm as a sensitive tool for disentangling these effects and assessing the distinct contributions of different components of vigilance.

In light of the relevant yet somewhat contradictory findings of Studies 1 and 2, and those observed in previous laboratory-based research (Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022) regarding the modulation of perceptual salience and task load on EV, we re-analyzed data collected across different samples and environments (i.e., lab and online) to gain a better and more solid understanding.
text.formatted: In light of the relevant yet somewhat contradictory findings of Studies 1 and 2, and those observed in previous laboratory-based research <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Luna, Barttfeld, et al., 2022)</ref> regarding the modulation of perceptual salience and task load on EV, we re-analyzed data collected across different samples and environments (i.e., lab and online) to gain a better and more solid understanding.

text.text: Thus, the main goal of this reanalysis was to assess the robustness of the perceptual salience and task load manipulations, and more importantly, their modulation over time-on-task on EV measured under the same procedure (i.e., the ANTI-Vea task) across the different samples.
