text.text: The present work analyzed how perceptual salience and task load independently and 974 jointly influence the EV decrement, using the ANTI-Vea task across three complementary 975 56 data sets.

Study 1 manipulated perceptual salience; Study 2 implemented a full factorial design with both salience and task load; and Study 3, a final re-analysis, replicated this design in a larger more diverse sample (n = 238) by combining both studies with data from previous work (Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Study 1 manipulated perceptual salience; Study 2 implemented a full factorial design with both salience and task load; and Study 3, a final re-analysis, replicated this design in a larger more diverse sample (n = 238) by combining both studies with data from previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Luna, Barttfeld et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, and in contrast to previous research, both target salience and task load were manipulated while maintaining all other aspects of the task, stimuli, and temporal parameters constant across conditions.

Across all three studies, the overall result showed that increasing perceptual salience consistently enhanced performance: higher salience levels were associated with higher hit rates, fewer FA, and greater sensitivity.
In Study 1, the high-salience condition was associated with a higher proportion of hits and a lower FA rate than the low-and standard-salience conditions.
Study 2 replicated and extended this pattern in a within-participant design, showing that salience affected EV even when combined with different levels of task load.
Finally, Study 3 confirmed the robustness of this effect in the pooled sample.
Critically, analyses on signal detection theory measures clarified the nature of the salience effect.

Higher perceptual salience was associated with largest sensitivity, indicating that participants were better able to discriminate signal from non-signal trials when the target displacement was more salient.
This graded pattern was especially clear in Study 3, where sensitivity was largest in the high-salience condition, followed by the standard-and lowsalience conditions.
Therefore, the salience manipulation was effective not only in changing direct performance measures, such as hits and FA, but also in modifying the discriminability of the EV signal.

This pattern is generally consistent with the idea that increasing the perceptual salience of critical signals reduces perceptual task demands and facilitates target detection (Helton & Warm, 2008; Warm et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This pattern is generally consistent with the idea that increasing the perceptual salience of critical signals reduces perceptual task demands and facilitates target detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Helton & Warm, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Warm et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, the findings also suggest that this interpretation should be qualified.
In Study 1, although high salience improved overall performance, sensitivity did not show the same time-on-task modulation observed in hits.
Moreover, the NASA-TLX results in Study 1 indicated that subjective workload did not significantly differ as a function of perceptual salience.
This suggests that increasing signal salience may improve perceptual discrimination without necessarily producing a corresponding reduction in perceived workload.
Task load, in contrast, showed a non-linear effect.
In line with the findings of Luna et al. (2022), participants performed better under dual-task conditions compared to both single and triple-task conditions.
text.formatted: In line with the findings of <ref type="bibr">Luna et al. (2022)</ref>, participants performed better under dual-task conditions compared to both single and triple-task conditions.

text.text: This inverted-U pattern aligns with mind-wandering hypothesis and resource control theory (Seli et al., 2018; Thomson et al., 2015), which suggest that moderate task complexity promotes sustained attentional engagement.
text.formatted: This inverted-U pattern aligns with mind-wandering hypothesis and resource control theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Seli et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>, which suggest that moderate task complexity promotes sustained attentional engagement.

text.text: Performance declined when tasks were either too simple (low stimulation) or too demanding (overload), likely due to disengagement or fatigue.

Moreover, a significant interaction between salience and task load was observed in Study 2 and the final summary reanalysis (Study 3): under low-salience conditions, performance was particularly impaired by high task load, while high salience mitigated this negative effect.
This underscores the importance of jointly considering perceptual and task load when designing vigilance tasks.
However, the signal detection analyses indicate that this interpretation should be substantially softened.
Task load did not produce a robust general effect on sensitivity.
In contrast, it clearly affected response bias.
Participants adopted the most conservative criterion in the triple-task condition, an intermediate criterion in the single-task condition, and the most liberal criterion in the dual-task condition.
Therefore, the differences observed in hit and FA rates across task-load conditions should not be interpreted as direct evidence of differences in signal discrimination.
Rather, they seem to reflect, at least in part, changes in response strategy.

The lower hit rates observed in the single-task condition should not be directly attributed to mind-wandering, just as the lower hit rates observed in the triple-task condition should not be directly attributed to resource depletion.
Although both mechanisms remain theoretically plausible, the present data do not allow us to distinguish them directly.

In particular, the absence of a clear task-load effect on sensitivity suggests that the task-load manipulation primarily influenced the criterion used to respond to the EV signal, rather than producing a strong change in the ability to discriminate the signal itself.
Subjective workload showed a partial dissociation from performance.

In Study 1, perceptual salience did not modulate NASA-TLX scores, despite clear improvements in hits and false alarms, suggesting that perceptual facilitation can enhance vigilance performance without reducing perceived task demand.

In contrast in Study 2, both perceptual salience and task load affected NASA-TLX scores: low salience and higher task load were experienced as more demanding, indicating that subjective workload is sensitive to global task demands.
However, and as mentioned, despite these performance effects, none of the manipulations influenced the vigilance decrement over time.
Performance declined steadily across all conditions, suggesting the involvement of additional factors beyond perceptual salience or task load.
Thus, the solid pattern of data observed across the three data sets is difficult to reconcile with current resource depletion hypothesis or mind-wandering hypothesis of vigilance.
A central finding across the present work is that neither perceptual salience nor task load robustly modulated the vigilance decrement over time-on-task.
In Study 1, the high-salience condition reduced the decrement in hits, but this pattern was not mirrored by a comparable modulation of sensitivity.

In Study 2 and Study 3, the analyses of A′ and B″ showed significant changes across blocks, but no significant interactions between block and perceptual salience, block and task load, or block, perceptual salience, and task load.
Thus, the manipulations affected the overall level of discrimination and response criterion, but they did not substantially alter the temporal trajectory of the EV decrement.
This pattern has important implications for theories of vigilance decrement.
First, it shows that a decrease in hit rates should not automatically be interpreted as a loss of sensitivity.
Changes in response criterion can produce similar patterns in hit and FA rates without necessarily implying that participants became less able to discriminate signals from non-signals.
Second, the findings suggest that models based solely on overload or underload may be insufficient to explain the full pattern of EV performance.

Task demands may influence both signal discriminability and response strategy, and these processes do not necessarily change in the same way over time-on-task (Thomson et al., 2015 (Thomson et al., , 2016).
text.formatted: Task demands may influence both signal discriminability and response strategy, and these processes do not necessarily change in the same way over time-on-task <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Thomson et al., , 2016</ref>).

text.text: An alternative interpretation of this pattern is offered by expectancy-based accounts of vigilance, which emphasize adjustments in response criterion rather than changes in perceptual sensitivity over time.

In modern vigilance tasks characterized by low signal probability, such as the executive vigilance trials of the ANTI-Vea, performance decrements may be strongly reflected in shifts toward a more conservative response bias, sometimes without a corresponding decrease in sensitivity (Gyles et al., 2023; Roman-Caballero et al., 2023; Thomson et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In modern vigilance tasks characterized by low signal probability, such as the executive vigilance trials of the ANTI-Vea, performance decrements may be strongly reflected in shifts toward a more conservative response bias, sometimes without a corresponding decrease in sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gyles et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roman-Caballero et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Thomson et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, participants may progressively adapt their response strategy to the rarity of critical signals, resulting in fewer responses to both signal and non-signal trials.
This account provides a parsimonious explanation for why the vigilance decrement persisted across conditions even when perceptual salience and task load changed overall performance.
At the same time, the persistence of the vigilance decrement across conditions leaves open the question of which mechanisms drive performance decline over time.
One relevant candidate is mind-wandering.
Numerous studies have shown that mind-wandering increases as time-on-task progresses, while task performance tends to decrease (Smallwood, 2010; Smallwood & Schooler, 2006 , Thomson, et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Numerous studies have shown that mind-wandering increases as time-on-task progresses, while task performance tends to decrease <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Smallwood, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Smallwood & Schooler, 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">, Thomson, et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: According to resource-control theory, attentional resources do not necessarily disappear over time; rather, the allocation of resources between task-related and task-unrelated activity is regulated by cognitive control (Thomson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: According to resource-control theory, attentional resources do not necessarily disappear over time; rather, the allocation of resources between task-related and task-unrelated activity is regulated by cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Thomson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, the ability to maintain task focus and suppress internal distractions may weaken, allowing attention to drift away from task goals.
However, the present studies did not directly measure mind-wandering during task performance.
Therefore, mind-wandering should be considered a plausible mechanism for future research rather than a demonstrated explanation of the present task-load effects.

The same caution applies to resource depletion: although the overload framework provides a useful account of how high task demands may impair vigilance, the current results do not show that the triple-task condition reduced sensitivity through a depletion of attentional resources.

Thus, the present findings are best interpreted as showing that perceptual salience and task load affect different components of EV performance, while the mechanisms underlying the time-on-task decrement remain to be directly tested.
The present findings have practical implications for the design of monitoring systems and tasks requiring sustained attention.

Vigilance decrement can lead to a wide range of consequences, from relatively mild effects such as missing a critical signal to severe outcomes including fatal car crashes (Baysari et al., 2008; Edkins & Pollock, 1997; Wundersitz, 2019).
text.formatted: Vigilance decrement can lead to a wide range of consequences, from relatively mild effects such as missing a critical signal to severe outcomes including fatal car crashes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baysari et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Edkins & Pollock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wundersitz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Increasing the perceptual salience of critical signals reliably improved detection performance and sensitivity without necessarily increasing overall task demands.
In addition, introducing moderate levels of task load may help sustain attentional engagement in monotonous or low-stimulation environments.
However, the present findings also indicate that improving raw detection performance does not necessarily mean that the vigilance decrement has been eliminated.
Even when perceptual salience improved sensitivity and task load modified response bias, neither manipulation robustly prevented the time-on-task decrement.
Therefore, applied interventions should consider not only whether signals are detected more often, but also whether users are changing their response criterion over time.
The findings regarding task load also have applied relevance.
The dual-task condition was associated with the least conservative response criterion, whereas the triple-task condition promoted the most conservative criterion.

Thus, moderate task demands may increase participants' willingness to respond to vigilance signals, but this should not be interpreted as evidence of improved sensitivity or as direct evidence for an optimal level of attentional resources.

In applied settings, reducing misses by encouraging a less conservative criterion may also increase the risk of FA, so the balance between sensitivity and response bias should be carefully considered.
The ANTI-Vea is available as an online, open-access platform (https://anti-vea.ugr.es/), which facilitates its implementation across a wide range of experimental and applied contexts.
text.formatted: The ANTI-Vea is available as an online, open-access platform (<ref type="url" target="https://anti-">https://anti-</ref>vea.ugr.es/), which facilitates its implementation across a wide range of experimental and applied contexts.

text.text: A key strength of the task is its modular structure, which allows different subtasks to be combined or isolated depending on the research question, enabling flexible referring to this specific class of task configurations.

Consequently, future studies should examine whether similar performance patterns and vigilance dynamics emerge under alternative single-, dual-, and triple-task conditions that involve different combinations of cognitive processes.
An additional limitation, the perceptual-salience manipulation was based on three discrete levels of vertical displacement.

This design was useful for comparing conditions of different perceptual difficulty and was consistent with the preregistered analyses of Studies 1 and 2, which focused on hits, FA, sensitivity, and response bias.
However, the present studies were not designed to estimate individual psychometric functions.
Although such analyses would provide a more fine-grained characterization of perceptual sensitivity and response bias, they were beyond the scope of the present design and analytic plan.

Future research should use psychometric-curve analyses to distinguish more precisely changes in perceptual sensitivity, internal processing noise, lapse rate, guess rate, and response criterion (Gyles et al., 2023; Roman-Caballero et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Future research should use psychometric-curve analyses to distinguish more precisely changes in perceptual sensitivity, internal processing noise, lapse rate, guess rate, and response criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gyles et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roman-Caballero et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A further limitation of this work is the absence of direct measures of mind-wandering and cognitive effort, which constrains a full understanding of the mechanisms underlying vigilance decrement.
Future research should incorporate self-report, behavioral, or physiological indicators to better characterize these processes and refine explanatory models.

Finally, although the final reanalysis enhanced generalizability by including a larger and more diverse sample, data were collected under controlled laboratory settings or instructed homebased protocols, predominantly involving young adult participants.
Replicating these findings in applied contexts and across broader populations would be essential to strengthen ecological validity.

Overall, results obtained using the ANTI-Vea task offer a sensitive assessment of EV and demonstrate that perceptual salience and task load influence vigilance performance in complex, interacting ways.

Integrating measures of mind-wandering and cognitive control in future studies could further advance understanding of how concurrent demands and temporal dynamics interact to shape attentional control during prolonged tasks.
 Performance (hits, FA, sensitivity and response bias) in vigilance tasks typically declines over time, posing risks in contexts that require monitoring the environment to detect critical stimuli.
 This study examined the roles of perceptual salience and task load in the vigilance decrement using the ANTI-Vea task.
 Perceptual salience robustly improved sensitivity, indicating better discrimination of signal from non-signal trials.
 Task load primarily affected response bias: participants adopted the most conservative criterion in the triple-task condition and the least conservative criterion in the dual-task condition.
 More salient stimuli and a moderate task load (dual-task) were associated with better performance.
 Neither perceptual salience nor task load altered the vigilance decrement over time.
 The findings highlight the importance of balancing perceptual stimulation and cognitive demands to optimize vigilance.

Data from 25 participants were collected at the University of Granada, Spain, where each participant received €60 for their participation, whereas the remaining 25 participants were from the National University of Córdoba, Argentina, and voluntarily participated in the study without receiving any economic or academic compensation.
Inclusion criteria were being between 18 and 35 years old, having normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and having access to a computer with an internet connection.
All participants volunteered to take part in this study and completed an online informed consent form at the beginning of the experiment.
The final sample included 45 participants: 21 from the National University of Córdoba (UNC, Argentina) and 24 from the University of Granada (UGR, Spain).
At UNC, 4 participants dropped out for unknown reasons.
At UGR, one participant did not complete all sessions and was excluded from analysis.

The study at UGR was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Granada (1188/CEIH/2020), whereas at UNC the study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychological Research (CEIIPsi -PE 41 v.2).
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (latest update in Brazil 2013).
Participants completed ten online sessions in total.

text.text: Whereas the re-analysis of pooled data from a large sample size increases the statistical power of observed outcomes, note that participants' assignment to experimental conditions was not randomized in the present re-analysis.
Therefore, the observed outcomes should not be considered as confirmatory, but rather exploratory.

We expect that this reanalysis can provide new empirical evidence concerning a more integrative understanding of how EV is influenced by different task demands (i.e., perceptual salience and task load) that can be manipulated either independently or simultaneously in between or within-participant designs.

This flexibility makes the ANTI-Vea particularly suitable for studying vigilance in applied domains such as sleep deprivation, fatigue, circadian rhythms, or workload management, where task demands can be adapted to reflect real-world operational constraints.

Moreover, its online format allows for large-scale data collection and remote testing, which is especially valuable for human factors research aiming to assess sustained attention under ecologically relevant conditions.
As such, the ANTI-Vea provides a versatile methodological framework that can be readily adapted to bridge laboratory-based vigilance research with applied and real-world settings

An important limitation is that the contradictory findings across studies may partly stem from differences in experimental design, as Study 1 employed a mixed-participant design whereas Study 2 used a within-participant design.

Mixed or between-participant designs are less sensitive to subtle effects and more susceptible to inter-individual variability, which may be particularly relevant when attempting to replicate prior work that predominantly used within-subjects approaches (Charness et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Mixed or between-participant designs are less sensitive to subtle effects and more susceptible to inter-individual variability, which may be particularly relevant when attempting to replicate prior work that predominantly used within-subjects approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Charness et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Another limitation of the present work is that task load was manipulated through qualitatively different task configurations rather than equidistant levels along a single quantitative dimension.

Accordingly, the single-, dual-, and triple-task conditions differed not only in the nominal "level" of load, but also in the specific cognitive demands they imposed, such as response inhibition or increased working memory load.
Within this framework, the inverted-U-shape performance function is offered as an interpretation of the patterns observed under these particular task-load conditions.
